messages.subject: comparison of random walk precision parameter between two models
messages.subject_clean: comparison of random walk precision parameter between two models
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am modelling population trends for different species using random walks, following the example set in Zuur's book.

I'm wondering if it makes sense to compare the precision parameter of the random walks between species as an indication of their variability, i.e. if we can expect certain species to change more abruptly between years than others. My main concern is that abundances are very different between species, and I'm not completely sure how that affects the comparability of the precision parameter.

In case more detail is needed, I model each species independently and my models look something like this:

comp <- ~ Intercept_p(1) + rw_species1(year, model = "rw2")

lik_p <- like(pa_df$biomass_species1~ Intercept_p +  rw_species1,
              data = pa_df,
              family = "gamma")

joint_m <- bru(comp,   lik_p)

I do the same for each species.

What do you think?  Hope this question is not too out of place.

Thanks,

Paula

messages.subject: Request for help
messages.subject_clean: Request for help
messages.body_plain:
Hi!
I'm very new to INLA and Bayesian stat. I'm trying to estimate prevalence of stunting by district through small area estimation. I tried to write code and generate result. Since District is in the spatial effect, I used random effect to determine prevalence by district (prevalence <-exp(random_effect)/(1+exp(random_effect$mean))).  But I'm not sure that I'm doing right or wrong. Can anyone help me to estimate prevalence by district adjusting for some variables using INLA package.

My code  is here
# construct neighbor list from shape files containing polygons
nb <- spdep::poly2nb(regions_shapefile,row.names = regions_shapefile$DISTRICT)

# Construct adjacent matrix
adj_matrix <- spdep::nb2mat(nb, style="B", zero.policy=TRUE)

# Keep names of column and rows same
colnames(adj_matrix)<-rownames(adj_matrix)

# define outcome variable
PRdata$outcome<-ifelse(PRdata$nt_ch_wast=="No", 0, 1)
PRdata2<-PRdata %>% filter(!is.na <http://is.na>(PRdata$nt_ch_wast))

# INLA model
# Define the INLA model formula
formula <- outcome ~Age+Sex+Rural_urban+ f(DISTRICT, model="besag", graph=adj_matrix,scale.model  = T)

# Fit the model with INLA, including weights
result <- inla(formula,
               family="binomial", weights = hv005/100000,
               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
               data=PRdata2)

# Examine results
summary(result)

# Fixed and random effects
fixed_effect <-result$summary.fixed
random_effect<-result$summary.random$DISTRICT

# Estimate prevalence for each districts
prevalence <-exp(random_effect)/(1+exp(random_effect$mean))

result_dt<-data.frame(DISTRICT=random_effect$ID, Prevalence=prevalence)

# join prevalence data with the shape file to plot
regions_shapefile<-regions_shapefile |>
  left_join(result_dt, by= "DISTRICT")

# Plot shape file of Nepal with districts and prevalence of stunting
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = regions_shapefile, aes(fill=Prevalence.mean))+
  xlab("Longitude") + ylab("Latitude")+
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.3) +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
                         pad_x = unit(0.75, "in"), pad_y = unit(0.5, "in"),
                         style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(79.9, 88.2), ylim = c(26, 30.5))+
  theme_bw()

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

My apologies for the vague description.

I'm possibly misinterpreting an approach or being led astray; I'm growing more doubtful as I grapple with the idea more. Just to clarify and close the loop, in case you have any better ideas.

A simplified version of the idea is conveyed at the link below, on page 16 and 17 (equation 7a, 7b, and 8)
https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/2016/wp16213.pdf

an individual property is represented as i

Current (as shown here https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=8ba35e5d6144e1c7f2ccb65826b2864514ea98e9):
Price(i) = Beta(s,t) + Beta(attributes)

Ideal (latent price index is the response; we can't create the response in this way due to heterogenous properties/sales and we want to leverage that to measure the latent price index) :
Price(s,t) - Price(s, t-1) = Beta(s,t) + Beta(attributes)

Potential work around (I think this is how I misinterpreted the IMF paper above):
Price(i) = ( Beta(s,t) - Beta(s,t-1) ) + Beta(attributes)
                  ^^ The price index ^^

The latter seems flawed because the Current approach adequately controls for spatial and temporal autocorrelation, and it isn't expected that
the rate of appreciation/depreciation is a primary driver of the current price; it's just that the rate of appreciation/depreciation is what we're trying to estimate across both space and time.

The way I'm addressing this now using the Current approach is calculating the index after modeling, using inla.mesh.project for each grouped time period (and mesh location), by converting to a raster (R) then calculating RIndex = Rt - R(t-1).

Thanks for all of your fantastic work!

messages.subject_clean: confounding problem of interaction terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I had a look at the paper "Age-space-time CAR models in Bayesian disease mapping" by Goicoa, Ugarte et.al <http://et.al>..

Therein they built the following model for mortality rates:

with \beta the intercept \phi_i a spatial Leroux random effect, \delta_j a age random effect (RW1) and \gamma_t a temporal random effect (RW1). The \eta`s are interaction terms of Type IV (space-age, space-time and age-time effects) with
covariance matrices given by the Kronecker product of the marginal covariances.

I would like to modify this model for mortality rates, by adding age as a fixed effect (factor) instead of a RW1 model, omitting the temporal random effect (RW1) and ending up with a spatial Leroux random effect and the three interaction effects, i.e.,

log r=\beta+ factor(age) +\phi_i+\eta^1+\eta^2+\eta^3.

Do you think this is still an identifiable/plausible/legit model? Because in Knorr-Held (2000) it is written that:
In general, however, we recommend omitting only those main effects that are not assumed to interact.

I wonder because for me it seems more interpretable if I add factor(age) instead of a RW(1) on age. Since a fixed effect tells me how much more certain age groups are affect by mortality than others. How would you interpret a RW1 model on age?

I am very much looking forward to your answer and already say thanks in advance.

Best,
Corinna

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] On the appropriateness of the 1D- SPDE on time series problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stanley,

yes, the range parameter controls the speed at which the correlation
function decays over time, just as the AR-parameter controls that same
thing. For AR(1), we can relate the correlation range R to the
AR-parameter a_1 by a relation of the form
a_1^R = fraction. E.g. with fraction = 1/10, R*log(a_1)=log(1/10) so
that R = log(1/10)/log(a_1) (assuming a_1 is positive, so that the
continuous time model exists), and R is the time-frame at which the
correlation goes down to 1/10.
For the continuous model, the correlation function is exp(-t/R) where
r is the time-lag, and exp(-t/R)=1/10 gives t = -R*log(1/10) as the
time-lag for which it reaches 1/10. So the R value isn't the same as
in the other relation, but the interpretation is similar; it's just
scaled by a constant.

One can parameterise the models to have exactly the same
interpretation: To find the continuous range parameter that gives the
same decay rate as the discrete model, consider
  a_1^R = exp(-R/param)
Then
  R*log(a_1) = -R/param
and
  param = -1/log(a_1)
(Note: the spde models use a heuristic definition of "range" that
doesn't exactly match this)

For AR(2), it's a bit more involved, but the same principle applies.

As for how this is linked to _observed_ values, it's important to note
that your interpretation only strictly holds when the AR() process is
observed _exactly_. A soon as some noisy observation model is added,
the strict "observations at 30 to 39 influences the fit at time 40"
becomes a bit wobbly as the _observations_ from 30 through 39 don't
tell the whole story. As a rule of thumb, that reasoning works, but
the details sometimes matter.
And as for observations "in the future", yes, if they are supplied,
they will be used. The estimation work on the model&data _as a whole_,
i.e. it does _not_ do sequential estimation.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Good evening,
I write because I have problems in inserting the covariates into my model. Before I insert the covariates in the model, I already correct for the missing values, however when then I run the model, for each covariate I get this error message:

"Warning in input_eval.bru_input(component[[part]$input, data, env = component$env,  :
  Model input 'cov3' for 'cov3' returned some NA values.
Attempting to fill in spatially by nearest available value."

I guess I’m doing something wrong, but I can’t figure out what because in my raster there are no NA.

Here my code:

### coastal_coniferous_woodland_freshwater_saltwater
cov3 = coastal_coniferous_woodland_freshwater_saltwater1
values = values(cov3)
cov3_val = values

cov3_SPDF = terra::rast(SpatialPixelsDataFrame(points = coordinates(cov3),
                                                data = data.frame(cov3 = values),
                                                proj4string = inla.sp_get_crs(mainland)))

values <- inlabru:::eval_spatial(data = cov3_SPDF,
                                 where = ips)

ips_sf <- fm_transform(ips,
                       crs = fm_crs(cov3_SPDF))

values2 <- bru_fill_missing(data = cov3_SPDF,
                            where = ips,
                            values = values)

cov3_SPDF = SpatialPixelsDataFrame(points = new_xy,
                                   data = data.frame(cov3 = as.vector(A%*% values2)),
                                   proj4string = inla.sp_get_crs(mainland))

cov3 = terra::rast(cov3_SPDF)

sum(is.na <http://is.na>(cov3))
class       : SpatRaster
dimensions  : 738, 561, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
extent      : 157.1959, 718.1959, 5910.398, 6648.398  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : +proj=utm +zone=30 +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0,0,0,0,0 +units=km +no_defs
source(s)   : memory
name        : sum
min value   :   0
max value   :   0

## Model

cmp_Atlas = ~ 0 + Intercept_PP_A(1,
                            mean.linear=0,
                            prec.linear= 1) +
                  SPDE_PP_A(main=geometry,
                            model=spde,
                            mapper = bru_mapper(mesh_medit)) +
                  cov4(main = cov4,
                       mean.linear = 0,
                       prec.linear = 1) +
                  Intercept_BER(1,
                                mean.linear=0,
                                prec.linear= 1) +
                  SPDE_BER(main=geometry,
                           model=spde,
                           mapper = bru_mapper(mesh_medit)) +
                  cov3(main = cov3,
                       mean.linear = 0,
                       prec.linear = 1) +
                  cov1(main = cov1,
                       mean.linear = 0,
                       prec.linear = 1) +
                SPDE_PP_BER_A(main=geometry,
                              copy="SPDE_PP_A",
                              fixed=F,
                              hyper=hyper_joint,
                              mapper = bru_mapper(mesh_medit))

formula_PP_Atlas <- geometry ~  Intercept_PP_A - 3 +
                                SPDE_PP_A +
                                cov4

formula_BER_Atlas <- geometry ~ Intercept_BER +
  SPDE_BER +
  SPDE_PP_BER_A +
  cov1 +
  cov3

likelihood_PP_Atlas <- inlabru::like("cp",
                                formula = formula_PP_Atlas,
                                domain = list(geometry = mesh_medit),
                                samplers = mainland,
                                data = final_data_all_Atlas[,3],
                                include = c("Intercept_PP_A",
                                            "SPDE_PP_A",
                                            "cov4"))

likelihood_species_Atlas <- inlabru::like("cp",
                                         formula = formula_BER_Atlas,
                                         domain = list(geometry = mesh_medit),
                                         samplers = mainland,
                                         data = final_data_ber_Atlas[,3],
                                         include = c("Intercept_BER",
                                                     "SPDE_BER",
                                                     "SPDE_PP_BER_A",
                                                     "cov1",
                                                     "cov3"))

fit_Atlas <- bru(components = cmp_Atlas,
           likelihood_PP_Atlas,
           likelihood_species_Atlas,
           options = list(verbose = F,
                          inla.mode  = "experimental",
                          control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
                          #bru_initial = list(Intercept_PP_A = - 1),
                          bru_max_iter = 10))

Thank you in advance

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for pcmatern, the hyperparameter output already contains the range and
std.dev <http://std.dev>. parameter posterior summaries, so inla.spde2.result() doesn't
provide much additional benefits (and if you do use it, note that is
by default has nominal.range and nominal.variance in the output, not
just log of range and variance).

For transforming precision to variance, be mindful of the fact that
expectations are not invariant under transformations, but quantiles
are; i.e. you can transform the quantiles as 0.5quant_variance =
1/0.5quant_precision
and 0.95quant_variance = 1/0.05quant_precision (your expression uses
an additional square, which is incorrect; precision is 1/variance, not
1/std.dev.).
But expectations do not transform like that; E(f(X)) != f(E(X)).  To
get the posterior expectation of the variance you'd need to use e.g.
 rr_variance_posterior_mean = inla.emarginal(function(x) 1/x,
result$marginals.hyperpar[["Precision for rr"]])

Finally, whether the variance of rr is interpretable as "the" nugget
depends on what's in your rr variable, so it's impossible to tell just
from the code. Also, if it does give a separate value for each
observation, it depends on the observation model as well; having both
an iid component and a Gaussian observation model, e.g. is too much.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Community,

I have some issues concerning the use of the "excursion" R package for calculating excursion sets.

I am working on a Bayesian joint model in a purely spatial context for fusing in-situ weather observations and model-based data. The model has been implemented with "inlabru".

I have tried to follow the available documentation online, but I have not found anything focusing on "excursions" and "inlabru".

1) I have run "inlabru" with the "return.marginals.predictor=TRUE":

bru(cmp1,lik_data,lik_era5,options=list(verbose=TRUE,control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)))->inla.out

2)  The I have used the bru output as an input for the "excursions" function. Specifically, for the "stack" parameter, I have used: " inla.out$bru_iinla$inla_stack" and name ="Predictor" (actually, I am not sure this is the right way to use the excursions function)

excursions.inla(inla.out,inla.out$bru_iinla$inla_stack,name="Predictor",u=-1,u.link=TRUE,alpha=0.05,method = "QC",type="<")->exc.mesh

3) Now I would like to interpolate the excursions output using the "continuous" function:

continuous(ex=exc.mesh,geometry=mesh_modello,alpha=0.05)->sets

In the above command, "mesh_modello" is the meshed employed for implementing the joint model.

Unfortunately, I get the following error message:

" The number of computed F-values (2502) must match the number of elements of the continuous geometry definition (1248)."

I would really appreciate some hints to finalize my analysis with "excursions" and "inlabru".

Thanks,
Guido

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your detailed explanation, it helped clarify a lot.

I wanted to give a bit more context on how I defined rr in my model. Essentially, rr represents the identifiers for the schools where data was collected (my geographical region points). Here's the relevant part of my code:

```
stk.e1 <- inla.stack(
  tag = 'point',
  data = list(y = dm$n, numtrials = dm$N),
  A = list(A, 1, 1),
  effects = list(
    s = indexs,
    rr = 1:length(dm$elevation_cat),
    data.frame(
      b0 = 1,
      x1 = dm2$elevation,
      x3 = dm2$open_def_cat,
      x2 = dm2$prec_cat
    )
  )
)
mod <- inla(
  formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = numtrials,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
  control.family = control.family(link = 'logit'),
  control.predictor = list(
    compute = TRUE,
    link = 1,
    A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)
  ),
  control.compute = list(config = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE, cpo = T),
  control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-7),
  num.threads = 7,
  verbose = F
)

```
Finally, my observational model is based on a binomial distribution where y is the number of successes (positive cases) and N is the total number of trials (children tested).

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I have a very small medical data (21 observation with 5 covariate). To make sure for the generalization, I would like to do LOOCV using inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv> but I don't know How to interpret the
  -mean(log(r$cv[1:number of observations])).
The model that I'm using is logistic and the formula is as follows:
result <- inla(response ~ BNS1 + BNS2 +
               BNS3 + Gender + log(Age) -1,
              family = "binomial", data = data,
               control.predictor = list(link =1))
When I don't use the log transformation for "Age" variable, result$summary.fitted.values$mean
produce NA values. So, my second question is  what is difference between log(Age) and Age in the model?

the data is belong to a scarce disease so It's very very small. Any recommendation about the generalization make me happy.

Thanks in advance for your help and time.

messages.body_plain:
Ok. Thanks a lot!

On Monday, 07 October 2024 at 19:37:50 UTC+2 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> if you change age from RW1 to a factor, then it would make sense to remove all
> interactions that involve age, so then its age + space + time + space x time ??
>
>
>
> On Mon, 2024-10-07 at 04:30 -0700, TheCorinna1994 wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I had a look at the paper "Age-space-time CAR models in Bayesian disease
> > mapping" by Goicoa, Ugarte et.al <http://et.al>..
> >
> > Therein they built the following model for mortality rates:
> >
> > model 8.png
> > with \beta the intercept \phi_i a spatial Leroux random effect, \delta_j a age
> > random effect (RW1) and \gamma_t a temporal random effect (RW1). The \eta`s
> > are interaction terms of Type IV (space-age, space-time and age-time effects)
> > with
> > covariance matrices given by the Kronecker product of the marginal
> > covariances.
> >
> > I would like to modify this model for mortality rates, by adding age as a
> > fixed effect (factor) instead of a RW1 model, omitting the temporal random
> > effect (RW1) and ending up with a spatial Leroux random effect and the three
> > interaction effects, i.e.,
> >
> > log r=\beta+ factor(age) +\phi_i+\eta^1+\eta^2+\eta^3.
> >
> > Do you think this is still an identifiable/plausible/legit model? Because in
> > Knorr-Held (2000) it is written that:
> > In general, however, we recommend omitting only those main effects that are

#weight predicted, in which survey effect of RWS31144108
Grid$weight <- exp(Grid$w.pm <http://w.pm> + M1_Zinb1$summary.fixed[[1]][1]  + log(50/1) + M1_Zinb1$summary.random$fSurvey[M1_Zinb1$summary.random$fSurvey$ID == "2019feb_187",]$mean)

And I determine the 95%CI:

    Betas           <- SimData[[i]]$latent[BetaRows]

messages.subject: solve mode.status issues with SL approximation

messages.body_plain:
Good morning

Please excuse me for the likely cross-posting with a similar issue I had opened privately with the helpdesk, hope this is the right place to ask.

INLA apparently fails to locate hyperparameters mode when the Simplified Laplace approximation is applied (similar problem with Laplace approx as well); specifically it results result$mode$mode.status == 2.

When the Gaussian approx with VB mean correction is used for the same model it runs just fine.
These are the priors used; the model is a multilevel bivariate ICAR with 3 connected components:

ctrl.family <- list(
  list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -4, prior = "loggamma", param = c(1e-3, 1e-3)))),
  list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -4, prior = "loggamma", param = c(1e-3, 1e-3)), skew = list(initial = -0.015, param = 4))))

Here is the function call (SL approx):

inla( y ~ 0 + CC1 + CC2 + CC3 +  X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 +
    f(idx.vector, model = inla.IMCAR.model(k = 2, W = W.scaled),
      extraconstr = list(A = A.constr, e = rep(0,6))),
  data = input_data, family = c("Gaussian","sn"),
  control.family = ctrl.family, control.fixed = ctrl.fix ,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(config = T, cpo = T, dic = T, internal.opt = F),
  num.threads = 1, inla.mode = "classic",
  control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", dz = 1e-6))

May I please ask what is this issue due to, and if  there is a way to fix it while still using the SL approximation?

Here I attach the R code, the full logfiles (VB: new version, SL: simplified Laplace in old version), and the input data to run the code.

Thank you in advance
Best regards
LC

messages.subject: Linear combination of predicted outcomes
messages.subject_clean: Linear combination of predicted outcomes
messages.body_plain:
I am examining:

(1) the predicted outcomes of a dataset (for individuals 1:n)

and wish to compare to predicted outcomes to

(2) a modified version of the data with an altered covariate across the same individuals.

I which to compare predicted outcomes (original versus modified) and find the probability that the original outcomes are higher the the ones from the modified dataset.

Below is an example using the random walk example provided in INLA documentation. Here I want a (non-sampling) way of computing Pr(y.hat > y.hat.preds).

Any help would be appreciated.

Thanks,

John

-------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)

rm(list=ls())
set.seed(1)

n <- 100
z <- seq(0,6,length.out=n)
y <- sin(z)+rnorm(n,mean=0,sd=0.5)
dat <- tibble(
    y=y,
    z=z
)

preds <- dat %>%
    mutate(
        y = NA,
        z=z+1
    )
dat.preds <- bind_rows(dat,preds)

f <- y ~ 1 +
    f(z,
      model="rw2",
      constr=TRUE,
      scale.model=TRUE
      ##hyper=list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec",param=c(1,0.01)))
      )

mod <- inla(
    f,
    data=dat.preds,
    family="gaussian",
    control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE)
)

N <- nrow(dat)
y.hat <- mod$summary.fitted.values[1:N,"mean"]
y.hat.preds <- mod$summary.fitted.values[N + 1:N,"mean"]

diff <- y.hat - y.hat.preds

Pr(diff > 0)???

its seems like the model is almost singular. it runs into issues immedidately,
complaining that the Prec matrix is (numerical) singular,  but the 'safe=T'
option rescue it. the results for VB looks ok.

the SL has more problems, as the internal representation is more fragile for
these `numerical singular models'. it still are able to rescue itself, when I
run it here, so I guess the advice would be to upgrade to R-4.4 and install the
most recent testing version. then retry

I would not recomment using the SL as the new take with the VB correction is
(almost uniformly) superior. my running times (1 thread) was 6 seconds compared
to 95, in favour of the VB

hope this helps
H

### since fitted values is a monotone mapping of the linear predictor,  then
### y.hat > y.hat.preds   < == >   lin.hat > lin.preds.hat
### or the other way around if the link is decreasing

### that mean you can use the linear combinations for the difference and then
check these ones

M <- matrix(0, N, 2*N)
for(i in 1:N) {
    M[i, i] <- 1
    M[i, i + N] <- -1
}
lc <- inla.make.lincombs(Predictor = M)

mod <- inla(
    f,
    data=dat.preds,
    family="gaussian",

    control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE),
    lincomb = lc
)
for(i in 1:N) {
    ## to make a quick approximation
    m <- mod$summary.lincomb.derived[i, "mean"]
    s <- mod$summary.lincomb.derived[i, "sd"]

    print(c(i,
            1-inla.pmarginal(0, mod$marginals.lincomb.derived[[i]]),
            1-pnorm(0, mean = m, sd = s)))

}

messages.subject: Potential Computational Speed up in INLA and inlabru
messages.subject_clean: Potential Computational Speed up in INLA and inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Dear inla team,

I am currently running a model that uses INLA within MCMC. The INLA model I am fitting is a simple spatial Poisson regression with the log rate driven by a Gaussian process on a regular grid.

Even though the computational time of INLA is pretty fast (with 8 cores, it takes roughly 1.8 seconds), putting it into a MCMC setting is still quite computationally costly: obtaining 10000 MCMC sample would require roughly 5 hours.

Are there any ways to further reduce the computational cost for INLA in this case?

Specifically, the only thing that I need from the Poisson regression model is the log-marginal likelihood and the posterior mode of the linear predictor (log-rate) at the spatial grid.

So I am wondering if there are inla options that I can set so that INLA only needs to compute the previously mentioned quantities to save time?

Thank you very much!

Best,
David

messages.body_plain:
you can try something like this. takes from from 12s to 8s in the example below.

Germany = cbind(Germany,region.struct=Germany$region)

formula3 = Y ~ f(region.struct,model="besag",graph=g, constr = T) +
               f(region,model="iid") + f(x, model="rw2")

tref <- Sys.time()
for(i in 1:10) {
    r =  inla(formula3,
              family="poisson",
              data=Germany,
              E=E,
              verbose = !TRUE,
              num.threads = "1:1")
}
print(Sys.time() - tref)

tref <- Sys.time()
r.prev <- NULL
for(i in 1:10) {
    r =  inla(formula3,
              family="poisson",
              data=Germany,
              E=E,
              verbose = !TRUE,
              num.threads = "1:1",
              control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb",
                                  control.vb = list(enable = FALSE)),
              control.compute = list(return.marginals = FALSE),
              control.mode = list(result = r.prev, restart = TRUE))
    r.prev <- r
}
print(Sys.time() - tref)

messages.subject: Use of survey sampling weights with SPDE in binomial likelihood models
messages.subject_clean: Use of survey sampling weights with SPDE in binomial likelihood models
messages.body_plain:
Greetings all.

I am working with typical survey datasets (DHS specifically), where we have individual level observations (e.g. women/children), together with the village ID (cluster/primary sampling unit) they come from, each village has a longitude and latitude, the region (district/county) they come from, a sampling weight (inverse of inclusion probability - all women in a village have same sample weight), and a variable of interest (typically binary) e.g. a question on whether a woman uses modern contraceptive methods, so the dataset structure looks:

# A tibble: 27,565 × 6
   district  villageID.  longitude   latitude   weight       indicator
   <fct>      <dbl>       <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>           <dbl+lbl>
 1 samburu  875      2121.          104.       0.244           1 [yes]
 2 kajiado     1184     -416.           96.6      1.02              1 [yes]
 3 laikipia    1069      1134.           95.8      0.717           0 [no]
 4 kajiado     1190      -144.           102.       1.21            0 [no]
 5 nairobi     1660      1101.           88.0      4.28            0 [no]

We are often interested in aggregating the data to the village level, or district level in order to compute the prevalence of the indicators, and make inference about the mean at the village of district level. For now I illustrate using the village level, and the two approaches that are commonly used: (NOTE: each village has a unique sampling weight, and a unique longitude and latitude for location)

First method: We incorporate the weighting into the number of trials and successes (caveat: since the weights are non-integer, we will have to round them off (or multiply by a scale and round-off )downstream so the they are integers, as binomial likelihood deals with strictly integer counts)

d1 <-  z |>
  group_by(villageID, district) |>
  reframe(
    success = sum(indicator * weight),
    trials = sum(weight)
  )

head:
  villageID district        success trials
      <dbl> <fct>             <dbl>  <dbl>
1       975 elgeyo.            3.67   7.80
2      1130 narok             14.8   28.4
3      1132 narok              5.01  10.6

Second method: We compute number of successes and trials by summing, and also retain the village sampling weight independently
d2 <- z |>
  group_by(villageID, district) |>
  reframe(trials = n(),
          success = sum(indicator),
          weight = unique(weight))

head:
villageID district        trials success weight

A tricky challenge for me is, what weights to use for pixels from the prediction grid, and so far my best bet is to assume a weight of 1 for all upsampled locations, when predicting to the rest of the upsampled pixels, (this is why I would wish to work with aggregation method 1, which omits the need for using weights downstream), is there any advice/best practise on this so far ?

I am able to supply datasets and codes for checking this.

Thanks in advance.

Hi,

Also, I have always regarded the INLA within MCMC paper as a “proof of concept” to show that INLA can also be used as a “device" to reduce the dimension of your model (by means of computing the marginal likelihood conditional on some hyper parameters) and to fit models that are not latent GMRF models. I think the this is a great feature of INLA that it is often neglected. In practice, I would use importance sampling (as mentioned in my previous e-mail), numerical integration [1,2] or a grid/CCD strategy [3].

Best,

Virgilio

messages.subject: formula interpretation - space and time
messages.subject_clean: formula interpretation - space and time
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about the interpretation of a particular formula. I am setting up the following model for bru():

form <- count ~ Intercept(1) +
  car_space_deviation(polygon_idx, model="besag", graph=g1, constr=T) +
  rw1_year_effect(year_idx, model="rw1",  constr=T,
             group=polygon_idx, control.group=list(model="besag", graph=g1, constr=T))

The way I understand this formulation, there is (term 1) a global intercept, (term 2) a CAR structured deviation from the global intercept per spatial polygon, and (3) a first-order random walk per polygon, where the random walk in a given polygon is influenced by 1st order neighbors according to a CAR structure. Is that interpretation correct?

If so, how is the info shared for the rw1? Is the value for t+1 for a focal polygon based on a mean that comes from the values at t from the focal polygon plus its neighbors?

Thanks for any clarification.

Best,
Tim

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] formula interpretation - space and time
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] formula interpretation - space and time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

the "group" feature defines a latent field with Kronecker product
precision/covariance structure. The interpretation in your case is
that the difference between the values at one timepoint and the next
is given by a spatial besag model, i.e. the random walk increments are
spatially correlated:
x_{t+1}(s) = x_t(s) + v_t(s)
where the increments v_t(s) are spatially correlated besag fields,
independent for each time point.

Your last guess isn't quite right, as that would involve a
non-kronecker precision structure.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Use same hyperparameters
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Use same hyperparameters
messages.body_plain:
here is a small example (without the group, but that is easy to add)

m <- 98
n <- 100
phi <- 0.99
x0 <- scale(arima.sim(n, model = list(ar = phi)))
eta <- c()
xx <- list()
for(i in 1:m) {
    xx[[i]] <- scale(arima.sim(n, model = list(ar = phi)))
    eta <- c(eta, x0 + xx[[i]])
}

s <- 0.01
y <- eta + rnorm(n*m, sd = s)

## we let x0 be replicate m+1

res <- inla(y ~ -1 +
                f(idx1, model = "ar1", nrep = m + 1, replicate = r1) +
                f(idx2, copy = "idx1", replicate = r2, nrep = m+1),
            data = data.frame(y,
                              idx1 = rep(1:n, m),
                              idx2 = rep(1:n, m),
                              r1 = rep(1:m, each = n),
                              r2 = rep(m+1, n*m)
                              ),
            family = "normal",
            control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(1/s^2),
                                                           fixed = TRUE))))

par(mfrow = rep(ceiling(sqrt(m)), 2))
plot(res$summary.random$idx2$mean[m*n + 1:n], x0); abline(a=0,b=1)
for(i in 1:m) {
    plot(res$summary.random$idx1$mean[(i-1)*n + 1:n], xx[[i]])
    abline(a=0,b=1)
}
plot(eta, res$summary.linear.predictor$mean)
abline(a = 0, b = 1)

Dear INLA group,

I am considering using a point process to deal with preferential sampling, inspired by Chapter 4 in the book ‘Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA.’

The log-Cox point process model deals with the point pattern (the locations). That is, the response variable is 1 for observations (representing the points) and 0 for mesh nodes:

y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))

I want to extend the locations to include sampling durations at each point. That means, for observations, y.pp would be positive continuous values. I plan to use a ‘Tweedie’ likelihood and set the offset E as usual. Is this possible? Really appreciate your guidance.

Thanks,

Ruby

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The point process likelihood setup is a very specific construction (or
rather, can be one of several equally specific constructions; the book
uses a different method than the implementation in inlabru, which is
based on the "Going off grid" paper.
What you're describing would either be a completely separate model
(there's no direct link between a Poisson point process likelihood and
the Tweedie distribution), or not a point process variation, but
rather a variation of an aggregated _count_ observation model, or a
third thing. Which it is depends on _precisely_ what you mean. Are the
"sampling durations" a measure of local sampling effort? Then you
don't have a Poisson point process. Or are they "an event that lasted
this long was observed at this location"? THen it may be a version of
a point process, possibly a "marked point process".
Before you've figured out precisely the _model_ you want is, it's
impossible to give advice on how to implement it.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
messages.body_plain:
OK, so the confusion is that you talked about the "sampling duration"
at each observed point, but the sampling effort is not a value
observed for each observation, but instead has to be known or modelled
for _every_ location in space.

A regular point pattern model is
  {y_i} ~ PoissonProcess(E \lambda(s))
with constant sampling effort E, or
  {y_i} ~ PoissonProcess(E(s) \lambda(s))
with spatially varying sampling effort E(s).

To estimate such models, you have to either known E(s), or be able to
model it using some kind of observations of it.
There have been different approaches to this in the literature, but
the easiest is if you have sampling effort information that isn't tied
to the observed points, but rather known or observed by other means.
Assuming that you're able to write a joint model for E(s) and \lambdas(s), then
  \eta_apparent(s) = \log(\lambda(s)) + \log(E(s))
is the \log of the _apparent_ point process intensity, i.e. of the
observed point pattern when the true point pattern would have
intensity \lambda(s),
and your observed point pattern is a conditional Poisson point process
  {y_i}|\eta_apparent ~ PoissonProcess(\exp(\eta_apparent(s)))

Such models can in principle be implemented with inlabru (see the LGCP
examples at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/articles.html),
as they are a variation of distance sampling models, where the
sampling effort is modelled as a function of distance to the observer,
independent of the true lambda.
In the preferential sampling setting, it's more likely that E has some
features in common with \lambda. The models are fundamentally
non-identifiable unless one can constrain the effort model somewhow.

What you mentioned about using a Tweedie observation model seems to be
a completely different approach that I can't help you with.

Finn

messages.subject: Dividing the contribution of a certain variable
messages.subject_clean: Dividing the contribution of a certain variable
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I built a SPDE model(y ~ varA + varB + f("spde"), family="binomial") for risk mapping.
VarA is an essential variable for explaining y, but is a variable related to the individual profile and is not needed for mapping the estimated risk. VarB is a geographical factor and an important for risk mapping.
I therefore attempted to caluculate the risk excluding the contribution of varA from the model.
However, "fitted values" obtained from the inla object did not match the sum of the contributions of intercept, explanatory variables and spatial effects.
Therefore, I could not identify whether "fitted values removed the contribution of varA" or "sum of the contributions of intercept, varB and spatial effects" was appropriate for mapping.

The R-code and the plot of the relationship between the caluculated values are described below.
Why are the "fitted values" obtained from inla object and the "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters not equal?
If my understanding of the "fitted value" in inla object is incorrect, would you tell me any ideas for determining the "fitted values", excluding the contribution of varA for mapping.

Thanks!!

Amy

↓↓↓ R code ↓↓↓

bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
                     offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
                     boundary = bd)
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))

stack <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = mydata$y),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
    data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)
  ),
  tag = "observations"
)

formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)

result <- inla(formula,
               family = "binomial",
               data = inla.stack.data(stack),
               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE, config = TRUE))

summary(result)

index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data

# "fitted values" obtained from inla object
fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]

intercept <- result$summary.fixed ["(Intercept)","mean"]
varA_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varA", "mean"] * mydata$varA
varB_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varB", "mean"] * mydata$varB

spatial_effect<-result$summary.random$spatial$mean
spatial_effect_contribution<-as.vector(A %*% spatial_effect)

# "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters
linear_predictor <- intercept + varA_contribution + varB_contribution + spatial_effect_contribution
fitted_manuals <- 1 / (1 + exp(-linear_predictor))

plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Dividing the contribution of a certain variable
messages.body_plain:
Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))

The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.
But due to the above fact, you wouldn’t get the same values anyway. You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
messages.body_plain:
In the point process itself, the observations are the locations of the points, and the sampling domain. 0/1 variables only come in when constructing the likelihood information for inla(), and whether that uses 0/1 variables or other values depend on the specific implementation. For example, in inlabru, the default Cox process likelihood construction has a single likelihood contribution for all of the observed points, with “y” for that contribution being equal to the total number of observed points, and zero for each spatial integration point contribution. Other equivalent approaches are possible.
Finn

messages.subject: Re: need help for "excursions" R package with "inlabru" output
messages.subject_clean: need help for "excursions" R package with "inlabru" output
messages.body_plain:
Hi Guido,

The problem is that you need to make excursions.inla compute the predictions at the mesh nodes to be able to use continuous. This was easy to set in base INLA using the stack and tag method, but it was less straightforward using inlabru. However, we now have a simple solution if you install the latest development versions of both inlabru and excursions from github.

The steps are as follows: You first add a likelihood in the bru call which contains NA observations at all mesh locations and you can add a tag for this (say tag = "pred"). You then call excursions.inla using the arguments prune.ind = TRUE, name = "APredictor" and ind = bru_index(result, "pred"), where "result" is the object returned by the bru call. After this you can use continuous as usual.

I am attaching a simple example comparing this bru method and the standard INLA method.

On Wednesday 9 October 2024 at 16:28:14 UTC+3 Guido Fioravanti wrote:
> Dear INLA Community,
>
> I have some issues concerning the use of the "excursion" R package for calculating excursion sets.
>
> I am working on a Bayesian joint model in a purely spatial context for fusing in-situ weather observations and model-based data. The model has been implemented with "inlabru".
>
> I have tried to follow the available documentation online, but I have not found anything focusing on "excursions" and "inlabru".
>
> 1) I have run "inlabru" with the "return.marginals.predictor=TRUE":
>
> bru(cmp1,lik_data,lik_era5,options=list(verbose=TRUE,control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)))->inla.out
>
> 2)  The I have used the bru output as an input for the "excursions" function. Specifically, for the "stack" parameter, I have used: " inla.out$bru_iinla$inla_stack" and name ="Predictor" (actually, I am not sure this is the right way to use the excursions function)
>
> excursions.inla(inla.out,inla.out$bru_iinla$inla_stack,name="Predictor",u=-1,u.link=TRUE,alpha=0.05,method = "QC",type="<")->exc.mesh
>
> 3) Now I would like to interpolate the excursions output using the "continuous" function:
>
> continuous(ex=exc.mesh,geometry=mesh_modello,alpha=0.05)->sets
>
> In the above command, "mesh_modello" is the meshed employed for implementing the joint model.
>
> Unfortunately, I get the following error message:
>
> " The number of computed F-values (2502) must match the number of elements of the continuous geometry definition (1248)."
>
>
> I would really appreciate some hints to finalize my analysis with "excursions" and "inlabru".
>
>
> Thanks,
> Guido
>
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I am currently using R version 4.3.3, and I have encountered issues after installing INLA according to the official documentation. Despite my efforts to configure my R and Rtools environment correctly, I have not been able to resolve the problems,which I have found to be common among other users as well.

Initially, I installed version INLA_24.03.29, which is compatible with R-4.3.3. However, I encountered the following error when attempting to use the library:

library(INLA)

This is INLA_24.03.29 built 2024-03-29 13:04:47 UTC.

Following that, I executed my code:

n = 100; a = 1; b = 1; tau = 100

z = rnorm(n)

eta = a + b*z

scale = exp(rnorm(n))

prec = scale*tau

y = rnorm(n, mean = eta, sd = 1/sqrt(prec))

data = list(y=y, z=z)

formula = y ~ 1 + z

result = inla(formula, family = "gaussian", data = data)

This resulted in the following error:

*** inla.core.safe: The inla program failed, but will rerun in case better initial values may help. try=1/1

Error in inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts,  :

The inla program call crashed.

Subsequently, I referred to the documentation which states that from version 23.05.30, INLA is built for R-4.3. For older R versions, it is necessary to install INLA versions compatible with each R version using the remotes package. I attempted to install version 23.05.30 as follows:

remotes::install_version("INLA",version="23.05.30",repos=c(getOption("repos"), INLA="https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing"), dep=TRUE)

Initially, I received an error indicating that the package could not be found. Upon further inspection of the link, I discovered that the actual package name was 23.05.30-1. I then downloaded the package locally and attempted to install it using:

install.packages("D:/Desktop/APC_BAPC_Package/R_packages/INLA_23.05.30-1.zip", repos = NULL, type = "win.binary")

After successfully loading the package, I ran my code again but encountered the following error:

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

I really appreciate your helpful comments.

I have modified the control.predictor to add "link=1" and run inla() to calculate the fitted values in consideration of the ”posterior distribution" using the R-code below.
However, the calculated fitted_values differ significantly from the values from the inla-result object.
On the other hand, the logit-transformed both values appear to be correlated.

I understand that the values will never be equal as they are derived from sampled values, but since the two values are so far apart and correlated (i.e. appear to have a constant added), I suspect that I'm missin an important element in my calculation procedure.

Could you please check the following code and plots?

Sincerely yours,

↓Rcode↓

bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
                     offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
                     boundary = bd)
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))

stack <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = mydata$y),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),

    data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)     ## !!! The variables used in the actual calculation are different from the previous one.

  ),
  tag = "observations"
)

formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)

result <- inla(formula,
               family = "binomial",
               data = inla.stack.data(stack),

               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))

summary(result)

index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data

# Fitted values obtained from inla object
fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]

# No. of sample
n_samples <- 1000

# sampling parameters from posterior distribution
posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, result)

fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]

  #Hyper parameters
  range_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Range for spatial"]
  sigma_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Stdev for spatial"]

  nu <- 1.5 #smooth parameter
  d <- 2

  kappa <- sqrt(8 * nu) / range_sample

  gamma_nu <- gamma(nu)
  gamma_nu_d2 <- gamma(nu + d / 2)
  tau_numerator <- sigma_sample * sqrt((2 * pi)^(d) * kappa^(2 * nu) * gamma_nu / gamma_nu_d2)
  tau <- 1 / tau_numerator

  theta1 <- log(tau)
  theta2 <- log(kappa)

  Q <- inla.spde.precision(spde, theta = c(theta1, theta2))

  # spatial random effect
  u_sample <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q))

  # fixed effect
  beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varA",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta2_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varB",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  # linear predictor(logit)
  eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * mydata$varA) + (beta2_sample * mydata$varB) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)

  fitted_samples[, i] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample))
}

fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)

# fitted values vs fitted manual
plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)

# calculate logit-transformed fitted values and fitted manual
logit_fitted <- log(fitted_values / (1 - fitted_values))
logit_manual <- log(fitted_manual / (1 - fitted_manual))

plot(logit_fitted, logit_manual)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.

The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
In other words:

beta1, beta2, range, sigma are a priori independent

The estimation model involves a field spatial1 with covariance parameters range, sigma, and the predictor is
  eta1=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial1
The observations are all linked to this eta1.

One can also imagine a second field spatial2 that has the same range and sigma as covariance parameters, and
  eta2=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial2

The fitted.values values output is based on 1/(1+exp(-eta1))
Your sampling procedure appears to target 1/(1+exp(-eta2))

Finn

Dear Finn,

Thank you for your helpful comments, again.

As you pointed out, I should use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample() as they are.
I have modified R-code as shown below, however, the discrepancy between fitted_values and fitted_manual(:calculated by myself) has not been solved as shown in the following plot.

Do you have any ideas about the cause?

Sincerely yours,

↓Rcode↓

bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
                     offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
                     boundary = bd)
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))

stack <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = mydata$y),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
    data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)     ## !!! The variables used in the actual calculation are different from the previous one.

  ),
  tag = "observations"
)
formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)

result <- inla(formula,
               family = "binomial",
               data = inla.stack.data(stack),
               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
               control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))

summary(result)

index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data

# Fitted values obtained from inla object
fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]

# No. of sample
n_samples <- 1000

# sampling parameters from posterior distribution
posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, result)

fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]

  # spatial random effect
  u_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("^spatial:", rownames(sample$latent)))]

  # fixed effect
  beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varA",rownames(sample$latent)))]
  beta2_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varB",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  # linear predictor(logit)
  eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * mydata$varA) + (beta2_sample * mydata$varB) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)

  fitted_samples[, i] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample))
}

fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)

# fitted values vs fitted manual
plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)

Hi,

to debug this, I would start by comparing the linear predictor outputs instead of the transformed linear predictors, and compare like-for-like, i.e.
do not compare an expectation to a median, but expectation-expectation ("mean") or median-median ("0.5quant").
Compare your sampled eta values to the summary.linear.predictor values.

Finn

On Mon, 28 Oct 2024 at 12:11, Emi Yamaguchi <e.ya...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Finn,
>
> Thank you for your helpful comments, again.
>
> As you pointed out, I should use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample() as they are.
> I have modified R-code as shown below, however, the discrepancy between fitted_values and fitted_manual(:calculated by myself) has not been solved as shown in the following plot.
>
> Do you have any ideas about the cause?
>
>
> Sincerely yours,
>
> ↓Rcode↓
>
> bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
> mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
>                      offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
>                      boundary = bd)
> spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
>   mesh = mesh,
>   prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
>   prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
> )
>
> A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))
>
> stack <- inla.stack(
>   data = list(y = mydata$y),
>   A = list(A, 1),
>   effects = list(
>     spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
>     data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)     ## !!! The variables used in the actual calculation are different from the previous one.
>
>   ),
>   tag = "observations"
> )
> formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)
>
> result <- inla(formula,
>                family = "binomial",
>                data = inla.stack.data(stack),
>                control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
>                control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))
>
>
> summary(result)
>
>
> index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data
>
> # Fitted values obtained from inla object
> fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]
>
> # No. of sample
> n_samples <- 1000
>
> # sampling parameters from posterior distribution
> posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, result)
>
>
> fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)
>
> for (i in 1:n_samples) {
>   sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]
>
>   # spatial random effect
>   u_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("^spatial:", rownames(sample$latent)))]
>
>   # fixed effect
>   beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]
>   beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varA",rownames(sample$latent)))]
>   beta2_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varB",rownames(sample$latent)))]
>
>   # linear predictor(logit)
>   eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * mydata$varA) + (beta2_sample * mydata$varB) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)
>
>   fitted_samples[, i] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample))
> }
>
> fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)
>
> # fitted values vs fitted manual
> plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)
>
>
> 2024年10月28日月曜日 20:36:45 UTC+9 Finn Lindgren:
> > In other words:
> >
> > beta1, beta2, range, sigma are a priori independent
> >
> > The estimation model involves a field spatial1 with covariance parameters range, sigma, and the predictor is
> >   eta1=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial1
> > The observations are all linked to this eta1.
> >
> > One can also imagine a second field spatial2 that has the same range and sigma as covariance parameters, and
> >   eta2=beta0+beta1*x1+beta2*x2+spatial2
> >
> > The fitted.values values output is based on 1/(1+exp(-eta1))
> > Your sampling procedure appears to target 1/(1+exp(-eta2))
> >
> > Finn
> >
> >
> > On Mon, 28 Oct 2024 at 11:31, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > for the spatial effect model your code samples (spatial|range,sigma), given a sample of (range,sigma|observations).
> > > The inla() output samples from (spatial|range,signa,observations), i.e. your code neglects to condition on the observations when sampling from the spatial field.
> > > To manually sample correctly from the latent field, the easiest is of course to just use the sampled values from inla.posterior.sample().
> > > I'm not sure why you didn't use those?
> > > To get the correct posterior samples manually, it's a bit messy, since they are also correlated with beta1 and beta2; that's what inla.posterior.sample() already handle.
> > >
> > > The interpretation of your samples seems to be what the model would say about a new realisation of the whole model, assuming that beta1 and beta2 are unchanged, but that "spatial" gets a new random realisation.
> > > If that's what you want, then you shouldn't compare it to the fitted.values output, as those are conditionally on the observations.
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mon, 28 Oct 2024 at 08:42, Emi Yamaguchi <e.ya...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Dear Finn,
> > > >
> > > > I really appreciate your helpful comments.
> > > >
> > > > I have modified the control.predictor to add "link=1" and run inla() to calculate the fitted values in consideration of the ”posterior distribution" using the R-code below.
> > > > However, the calculated fitted_values differ significantly from the values from the inla-result object.
> > > > On the other hand, the logit-transformed both values appear to be correlated.
> > > >
> > > > I understand that the values will never be equal as they are derived from sampled values, but since the two values are so far apart and correlated (i.e. appear to have a constant added), I suspect that I'm missin an important element in my calculation procedure.
> > > >
> > > > Could you please check the following code and plots?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Sincerely yours,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > ↓Rcode↓
> > > >
> > > > bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
> > > > mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
> > > >                      offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
> > > >                      boundary = bd)
> > > > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
> > > >   mesh = mesh,
> > > >   prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
> > > >   prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))
> > > >
> > > > stack <- inla.stack(
> > > >   data = list(y = mydata$y),
> > > >   A = list(A, 1),
> > > >   effects = list(
> > > >     spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
> > > >     data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)     ## !!! The variables used in the actual calculation are different from the previous one.
> > > >   ),
> > > >   tag = "observations"
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)
> > > >
> > > > result <- inla(formula,
> > > >                family = "binomial",
> > > >                data = inla.stack.data(stack),
> > > >                control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
> > > >                control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))
> > > >
> > > > summary(result)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data
> > > >
> > > > # Fitted values obtained from inla object
> > > > fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]
> > > >
> > > > # No. of sample
> > > > n_samples <- 1000
> > > >
> > > > # sampling parameters from posterior distribution
> > > > posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, result)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)
> > > >
> > > > for (i in 1:n_samples) {
> > > >   sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]
> > > >
> > > >   #Hyper parameters
> > > >   range_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Range for spatial"]
> > > >   sigma_sample <- sample$hyperpar["Stdev for spatial"]
> > > >
> > > >   nu <- 1.5 #smooth parameter
> > > >   d <- 2
> > > >
> > > >   kappa <- sqrt(8 * nu) / range_sample
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >   gamma_nu <- gamma(nu)
> > > >   gamma_nu_d2 <- gamma(nu + d / 2)
> > > >   tau_numerator <- sigma_sample * sqrt((2 * pi)^(d) * kappa^(2 * nu) * gamma_nu / gamma_nu_d2)
> > > >   tau <- 1 / tau_numerator
> > > >
> > > >   theta1 <- log(tau)
> > > >   theta2 <- log(kappa)
> > > >
> > > >   Q <- inla.spde.precision(spde, theta = c(theta1, theta2))
> > > >
> > > >   # spatial random effect
> > > >   u_sample <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q))
> > > >
> > > >   # fixed effect
> > > >   beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]
> > > >   beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varA",rownames(sample$latent)))]
> > > >   beta2_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("varB",rownames(sample$latent)))]
> > > >
> > > >   # linear predictor(logit)
> > > >   eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * mydata$varA) + (beta2_sample * mydata$varB) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)
> > > >
> > > >   fitted_samples[, i] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample))
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)
> > > >
> > > > # fitted values vs fitted manual
> > > > plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)
> > > >
> > > > # calculate logit-transformed fitted values and fitted manual
> > > > logit_fitted <- log(fitted_values / (1 - fitted_values))
> > > > logit_manual <- log(fitted_manual / (1 - fitted_manual))
> > > >
> > > > plot(logit_fitted, logit_manual)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > 2024年10月26日土曜日 1:12:21 UTC+9 Finn Lindgren:
> > > > > Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,
> > > > > E(g(X)) is not equal to g(E(x))
> > > > >
> > > > > The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.
> > > > > But due to the above fact, you wouldn’t get the same values anyway. You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.
> > > > >
> > > > > Finn
> > > > >
> > > > > > On 25 Oct 2024, at 17:04, Emi Yamaguchi <e.ya...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ﻿Dear INLA group,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I built a SPDE model(y ~ varA + varB + f("spde"), family="binomial") for risk mapping.
> > > > > > VarA is an essential variable for explaining y, but is a variable related to the individual profile and is not needed for mapping the estimated risk. VarB is a geographical factor and an important for risk mapping.
> > > > > > I therefore attempted to caluculate the risk excluding the contribution of varA from the model.
> > > > > > However, "fitted values" obtained from the inla object did not match the sum of the contributions of intercept, explanatory variables and spatial effects.
> > > > > > Therefore, I could not identify whether "fitted values removed the contribution of varA" or "sum of the contributions of intercept, varB and spatial effects" was appropriate for mapping.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The R-code and the plot of the relationship between the caluculated values are described below.
> > > > > > Why are the "fitted values" obtained from inla object and the "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters not equal?
> > > > > > If my understanding of the "fitted value" in inla object is incorrect, would you tell me any ideas for determining the "fitted values", excluding the contribution of varA for mapping.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks!!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Amy
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ↓↓↓ R code ↓↓↓
> > > > > >
> > > > > > bd<-as(polygon,"Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
> > > > > > mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = st_coordinates(mydata), max.edge = c(1,5)*50,
> > > > > >                      offset=c(1,5)*50, cutoff = 5,
> > > > > >                      boundary = bd)
> > > > > > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
> > > > > >   mesh = mesh,
> > > > > >   prior.range = c(10, 0.01),
> > > > > >   prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
> > > > > > )
> > > > > >
> > > > > > A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = st_coordinates(mydata))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > stack <- inla.stack(
> > > > > >   data = list(y = mydata$y),
> > > > > >   A = list(A, 1),
> > > > > >   effects = list(
> > > > > >     spatial = inla.spde.make.index("spatial", spde$n.spde),
> > > > > >     data.frame(varA = mydata$varA, varB = mydata$varB)
> > > > > >   ),
> > > > > >   tag = "observations"
> > > > > > )
> > > > > >
> > > > > > formula <- y ~ 1 + varA + varB + f(spatial, model = spde)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > result <- inla(formula,
> > > > > >                family = "binomial",
> > > > > >                data = inla.stack.data(stack),
> > > > > >                control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute = TRUE),
> > > > > >                control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE, config = TRUE))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > summary(result)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > index <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag = "observations")$data
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # "fitted values" obtained from inla object
> > > > > > fitted_values <- result$summary.fitted.values$mean[index]
> > > > > >
> > > > > > intercept <- result$summary.fixed ["(Intercept)","mean"]
> > > > > > varA_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varA", "mean"] * mydata$varA
> > > > > > varB_contribution <- result$summary.fixed["varB", "mean"] * mydata$varB
> > > > > >
> > > > > > spatial_effect<-result$summary.random$spatial$mean
> > > > > > spatial_effect_contribution<-as.vector(A %*% spatial_effect)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # "fitted values" calculated based on the estimated parameters
> > > > > > linear_predictor <- intercept + varA_contribution + varB_contribution + spatial_effect_contribution
> > > > > > fitted_manuals <- 1 / (1 + exp(-linear_predictor))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)
> > > > > >

Thanks a lot.
I used the median fitted_values ('0.5quant').
As a result, both expectations appear to be more clearly correlated (plot1), the both logit values appear to shift by 8 overall (plot2).

Do you have any ideas about the cause?

Sincerely yours,

> > > > > > Without going into the details, it’s likely due to the fundamental fact that unless you have a linear mapping,

> > > > > > The fitted-values output takes your nonlinear link function into account if you specify link=1 in control.predictor. You didn’t, so I guess your fitted.values are actually the same as linear.predictor.

You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

messages.body_plain:
You will get minor differences due to the parallelisation done, where the number
of threads used, and how they are used, make a small difference. this is
controlled by the run-time system outside of our control.

if you want exactly the same results, you can get that with

	inla.setOption(num.threads = 1, internal.opt = FALSE)

(where internal.opt might chose different algorithms for doing stuff based on
timing, which may results in different algs doing the same thing, which will
give epsilon different results)

the attached is what you get with the options above

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

Thanks all.
I built a SPDE model using a dummy data, and a similar discrepancy of expectations was appeared.
On the other hand, the discrepancy was not appeared in the expectations from basic inla model(= without s).

I'm afraid of a lack of any augument about spatial random effect.
I apologise for the repetition, but I would be pleased to check when it is convenient for you.

Sincerely yours,

↓R cord↓

set.seed(2389)

data(SPDEtoy)
SPDEtoy$C<-rbinom(200,1,0.05)
SPDEtoy$var<-rnorm(200,5,1.5)
coords <- as.matrix(SPDEtoy[,1:2])

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(coords, max.edge=c(0.092, 0.2))
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha=2)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords)

stk_bin <- inla.stack(data=list(C=SPDEtoy$C), A=list(A,1),
                      effects=list(i=1:spde$n.spde,
                                   var=SPDEtoy$var), tag='bin')

res_bin <- inla(C ~ var + f(i, model=spde),family="binomial",
             data=inla.stack.data(stk_bin),
             control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk_bin),compute=TRUE,link=1),

             control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))

summary(res_bin)

index<-inla.stack.index(stk_bin, tag = "bin")$data
fitted_values<-res_bin$summary.fitted.values$`0.5quant`[index]

# No. of sample
n_samples <- 1000

# samples from posterior distributions
posterior_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, res_bin)

fitted_samples <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  sample <- posterior_samples[[i]]

  # fixed effect
  beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("var",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  #spatial random effect
  u_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("^i:", rownames(sample$latent)))]

  # linear predictor
  eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * SPDEtoy$var) + as.vector(A %*% u_sample)

  # transform to probability
  fitted_samples[, i] <- (1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample)))

}

fitted_manual <- rowMedians(fitted_samples)

# Compare the expectations
plot(fitted_values, fitted_manual)
hist(fitted_values,breaks = seq(0,1,0.005),col=rgb(1, 0, 0, alpha=0.5),xlim = c(0,1))
hist(fitted_manual,breaks = seq(0,1,0.005),col=rgb(0, 0, 1, alpha=0.5),xlim = c(0,1),add=TRUE)

##Without spatial effect

res_bin_nonsp <- inla(C ~ var ,family="binomial",
                      data=SPDEtoy, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,link=1),

                      control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE,config = TRUE))

summary(res_bin_nonsp)

fitted_values_nonsp<-res_bin_nonsp$summary.fitted.values$`0.5quant`[index]

posterior_samples_nonsp <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, res_bin_nonsp)

fitted_samples_nonsp <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(index), ncol = n_samples)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {

  sample <- posterior_samples_nonsp[[i]]

  # Fixed effect

  beta0_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("(Intercept)",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  beta1_sample <- sample$latent[which(grepl("var",rownames(sample$latent)))]

  # linear predictor
  eta_sample <- beta0_sample + (beta1_sample * SPDEtoy$var)

  fitted_samples_nonsp[, i] <- (1 / (1 + exp(-eta_sample)))

}

fitted_manual_nonsp <- rowMedians(fitted_samples_nonsp)

# Compare the expectations
plot(fitted_values_nonsp, fitted_manual_nonsp)
hist(fitted_values_nonsp,breaks = seq(0,0.25,0.005),col=rgb(1, 0, 0, alpha=0.5),xlim = c(0,0.25))
hist(fitted_manual_nonsp,breaks = seq(0,0.25,0.005),col=rgb(0, 0, 1, alpha=0.5),xlim = c(0,0.25),add=TRUE)

You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. messages.body_plain:
Please redo your last test with proper handling of the intercept. When using an A-matrix, you must not use the automated intercept. Remove it with 0+ in the formula, and add an explicit Intercept term in the formula and in the stack construction.
Perhaps that’s also the issue in your original model? But from what I recall, inla() should be giving a warning about this. Does it not?
Finn

You have to decide if you want the posterior expectation of the linear predictor transformed, or the expectation of the transformed linear predictor. Or something, such as the transformation of the posterior medians, that _are_ preserved through (monotonic) nonlinear transformation. In short, you have to think in terms of probability distributions, not “point estimators”.

messages.subject: Joint model accounting for preferential sampling failed
messages.subject_clean: Joint model accounting for preferential sampling failed
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I developed a joint model (Poisson point process and Tweedie) to deal with preferential sampling.

The model worked well when:
form <- y ~ -1 + y.b0 + e.b0 +
  f(ves.y, model="iid", hyper=list(theta=list(param=c(0.1,0.1))), constr=TRUE) +
  f(yq.y, model="rw1", hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.5,0.01))), scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(sy.0, model=spde) +

  f(yq.e, model="rw1", hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.5,0.01))), scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(se.0, model=spde) +
  f(yq.ey, copy="yq.y", fixed=FALSE, hyper=hypercopy) +
  f(sey.0, copy="sy.0", same.as <http://same.as>="yq.ey", fixed=FALSE, hyper=hypercopy)

res <- inla(form, family=c("tweedie", "poisson"),
            data=inla.stack.data(stk.all),
            E = inla.stack.data(stk.all)$e,
            control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, config = TRUE),
            control.inla=list(strategy='gaussian', int.strategy='eb'),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.all), compute=TRUE, link=inla.stack.data(stk.all)$link),
            num.threads=20, keep=TRUE, verbose=TRUE, debug=TRUE, safe=FALSE)

But failed when I added spatiotemporal effects:
form_new <- y ~ -1 + y.b0 + e.b0 +
  f(ves.y, model="iid", hyper=list(theta=list(param=c(0.1,0.1))), constr=TRUE) +
  f(yq.y, model="rw1", hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.5,0.01))), scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(sy.0, model=spde) +
  f(sy.1, model=spde, group=sy.1.group, control.group=list(model="ar1", hyper=rho_cp, scale.model=TRUE)) +

  f(yq.e, model="rw1", hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.5,0.01))), scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE) +
  f(se.0, model=spde) +
  f(se.1, model=spde, group=se.1.group, control.group=list(model="ar1", hyper=rho_cp, scale.model=TRUE)) +
  f(yq.ey, copy="yq.y", fixed=FALSE, hyper=hypercopy) +
  f(sey.0, copy="sy.0", same.as <http://same.as>="yq.ey", fixed=FALSE, hyper=hypercopy) +
  f(sey.1, copy="sy.1", same.as <http://same.as>="yq.ey", group=sey.1.group, fixed=FALSE, hyper=hypercopy)

I got lots of errors like "GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=xxxx". I appreciate any comments.

Thanks,
Ruby

messages.subject: Spatial binomial model overfitting
messages.subject_clean: Spatial binomial model overfitting
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I am trying to fit a simple binomial model with bym2 prior specification to estimate prevalence. My issue is the resultant fitted values from the model are identical to the crude prevalence values. I had hoped some Bayesian spatial shrinkage/smoothing would happen but this does not seem to be the case. I am not sure if it is because of the code I am using or if the data will not allow for it. I tried various priors and this is still an issue. I think the model is overfitting the data.

I have run examples from different textbooks and this issue does not appear. I have attached a simple reprex for you to see. Your assistance is appreciated.

Kind regards,
John

Hello,

I'm new here (and also a new R-INLA user). I'm interesting in occupancy models, and I'm trying to reproduce the simulations and the promising model shown in Belmont et al (2024) (here <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14422> and here <https://arxiv.org/html/2403.10680v1#bib.bib9>). However, I found the same issues as Claire Lay. I must say that the issues persisted after updating the packages (note in my session info that I'm using the last Matrix package version 1.7-1).
Digging a bit more on the issue I found this documentation <https://tomcat.heanet.ie/mirrors/cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Matrix/vignettes/Design-issues.pdf> that, as far I can understand, show that the conversion from different classes of sparse matrices should be somehow straightforward (e.g. from 'dgCMatrix' to 'dCsparseMatrix', which is required for R-INLA) using the Matrix package. However, when searching for the classes of sparse matrices available in the Matrix package (by typing getClass("dgCMatrix") in R), I didn't find any corresponding to 'dCsparseMatrix' (see the list below). So I'll ask two silly questions:

Should this mismatch be the source of the original issue? And how to fix it?
My R code is attached in any case.

Best regards,

Andre

messages.subject_clean: Informative prior for positive only expected value
messages.body_plain:
I have been trialling a model on species counts (count data from 0-60). I want to include what I think should be an informative prior to ensure that the expected values are all positive and potentially bound at an upper limit of 60. I just can't seem to figure out where in the code I can state this or how to go about it. I am currently using pc priors see code below. Does anyone have any advise or resources I could look into? Thanks in advance

inla.setOption(scale.model.default = TRUE)

U <- 0.1
hyper.prec = list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec",
                               param = c(U, 0.05)))
f<- species ~ var1 + var2 + Var3*Var4 +
  f(Var5, Var6, model = "rw2", cyclic=TRUE, hyper = hyper.prec)

I<- inla(f, control.predictor = list(
  compute = TRUE,
  quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)),
  control.compute = list(config = TRUE,dic = TRUE),
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
  data = dat, verbose=FALSE)
